articles.title: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
articles.summary: The three security objectives most controls protect, and why incidents are usually described by which of them was affected.

sections.heading: The three objectives
paragraphs: Confidentiality means information is only disclosed to authorised people and systems. Integrity means information and systems are not altered in unauthorised ways. Availability means authorised users can access systems and data when they need them.

sections.heading: Using the triad in practice
bullets: Data theft (IR-2026-006) is a confidentiality impact
A cleared audit log (IR-2026-002) affects the integrity of evidence
Ransomware (IR-2026-004) hits availability, and with data theft, confidentiality too

sections.heading: Beyond the triad
paragraphs: Many programmes also track authenticity, accountability and non-repudiation. These ideas sit behind logging, strong authentication and digital signatures.

practice.label: See impact classification in the incident cases

articles.title: Defence in depth
articles.summary: Layering independent controls so that one failure does not lead to a breach.

sections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: No single control is perfect. Defence in depth puts several independent layers in an attacker's way (identity, endpoint, network, application, data and monitoring), so the failure of one layer is caught or limited by another.

sections.heading: Seen in the case studies
bullets: Mail filtering missed a password-protected archive, but endpoint telemetry still caught Office spawning PowerShell
EDR isolation failed silently, and a switch-port shutdown contained the host instead
Forwarded logs survived the attacker clearing the domain controller's log

sections.heading: Design tip
paragraphs: Make layers genuinely independent. Two controls that depend on the same credential or the same agent fail together.

articles.title: How a Security Operations Centre works
articles.summary: Roles, the alert lifecycle and the measures SOCs use to understand their own performance.

sections.heading: Typical structure
paragraphs: Many SOCs organise analysts in tiers. Tier 1 triages incoming alerts, Tier 2 investigates confirmed suspicious activity, and Tier 3 or incident responders handle complex incidents, threat hunting and detection improvement. Smaller teams combine these roles.

sections.heading: Alert lifecycle
bullets: Detection: a rule or analytic raises an alert
Triage: is it real, how severe, and what is affected?
Investigation: scope, root cause, related activity
Response: containment, eradication, recovery
Feedback: tune the detection and record lessons learned

sections.heading: Useful measures
paragraphs: Commonly tracked measures include mean time to detect, mean time to respond, false-positive rate per rule, and coverage of important techniques and log sources. Measures should drive improvement, not alert-closing speed for its own sake.

articles.title: A repeatable alert-triage method
articles.summary: Five questions that turn an alert into a decision in a few minutes.

sections.heading: The questions
bullets: What exactly fired, and what does the rule look for?
Who and what is involved: user, host, asset criticality, source IP reputation?
What happened just before and after on the same host or account?
Is there a benign explanation (change ticket, known tool, scheduled job)?
What is the impact if this is real, and how urgent is it?

sections.heading: Document as you go
paragraphs: Record the evidence you checked, not just the conclusion. A good triage note lets the next analyst repeat your reasoning and helps you tune noisy rules later.

sections.heading: Escalate or close
paragraphs: Escalate when impact or uncertainty is high. Close as a false positive only when you can name the benign cause, and feed that back into the rule's filters.

practice.label: Pivot from an alert to raw logs

articles.title: Essential log sources for detection
articles.summary: The telemetry that supports most investigations and detections, and what each source is good for.

sections.heading: Windows
bullets: Security log: logons (4624), failed logons (4625), special privileges (4672), account creation (4720), audit log cleared (1102)
Process creation with command line (4688), or Sysmon event 1
PowerShell script block logging (event 4104)

sections.heading: Beyond the endpoint
bullets: Identity provider sign-ins, including MFA results
DNS resolver logs: which host asked for which domain
Proxy and firewall logs: destinations, bytes and actions
Web server access logs for public applications
Cloud audit logs (control-plane activity)

sections.heading: Practical advice
paragraphs: Collect less but collect well: the right events with command lines and correct timestamps beat everything at low quality. Forward logs off the host quickly so an attacker cannot erase them.

practice.label: Explore 8 log types in the SIEM

articles.title: Hardening and secure baselines
articles.summary: Reducing attack surface with consistent, verifiable configuration.

sections.heading: Start from a baseline
paragraphs: Community baselines such as the CIS Benchmarks describe secure settings for operating systems, cloud services and applications. Adopt one, document justified deviations and measure drift.

sections.heading: High-value settings
bullets: Remove local admin rights from everyday accounts
Disable unused services (the Print Spooler on domain controllers is a known example)
Block macros from the internet and restrict script interpreters
Enforce logging settings as part of the baseline

sections.heading: Verify continuously
paragraphs: Configuration drifts. Automated compliance scans and configuration management keep the baseline real rather than aspirational.

articles.title: Identity security and phishing-resistant MFA
articles.summary: Why identity is the main attack surface, and which controls actually stop modern credential attacks.

sections.heading: Why identity
paragraphs: Several case studies in this platform start with identity: password spraying, help-desk impersonation, session-cookie theft and service accounts with weak passwords. Valid credentials let attackers blend in.

sections.heading: Controls that matter
bullets: Phishing-resistant authenticators (FIDO2 security keys, platform passkeys, certificate-based) resist credential and code phishing
Remove legacy authentication protocols that bypass MFA
Separate administrative accounts and use privileged access workstations
Strong identity checks for password and MFA resets

sections.heading: Monitor
paragraphs: Alert on new MFA device registration, impossible travel, sign-ins after many failures, and service accounts logging on interactively.

articles.title: Hypothesis-driven threat hunting
articles.summary: Proactively searching for attacker activity that has not triggered an alert.

sections.heading: The hunting loop
bullets: Form a hypothesis, e.g. 'an attacker uses DNS TXT records for C2 in our network'
Identify the data needed to test it
Query and analyse, looking for outliers
Confirm or reject, and record what you learned
Turn confirmed patterns into detections

sections.heading: Hunt up the Pyramid of Pain
paragraphs: David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks indicators by how costly they are for an adversary to change. Hash values and IP addresses are trivial for attackers to change, while tools and TTPs (tactics, techniques and procedures) are expensive. Hunts and detections aimed at behaviour last longer.

practice.label: Hunt in the SIEM log explorer

articles.title: Using MITRE ATT&CK for hunting and coverage
articles.summary: Turning a knowledge base of adversary behaviour into hunt plans and coverage maps.

sections.heading: What ATT&CK is
paragraphs: MITRE ATT&CK is a publicly available knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. Tactics are the adversary's goals (for example credential access); techniques are how they achieve them (for example LSASS memory dumping).

sections.heading: Practical uses
bullets: Map existing detections to techniques to see gaps
Pick techniques used by actors relevant to your sector and hunt for them
Describe incidents in a shared vocabulary

sections.heading: Caution
paragraphs: A technique marked 'covered' rarely means every procedure is detected. Record which data source and which variant each detection handles.

articles.title: The detection engineering lifecycle
articles.summary: Treating detections as code: requirements, development, testing, deployment and maintenance.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
bullets: Requirement: a threat or technique worth detecting, and the data available
Development: write the logic, often in a portable format such as Sigma
Testing: run against known-good and known-bad data
Deployment: version control, review, rollout
Maintenance: track false positives, tune, retire stale rules

sections.heading: Test data matters
paragraphs: A rule that has never matched a true positive is untested. Keep sample events for each rule and run them automatically, which is what this platform's test suite does for its Sigma library.

practice.label: Edit and test a Sigma rule

articles.title: Measuring and reducing false positives
articles.summary: Keeping detections trustworthy without blinding the SOC.

sections.heading: Measure first
paragraphs: Track, per rule, how many alerts were true positives, benign true positives (real activity that was allowed) and false positives. Without that data, tuning is guesswork.

sections.heading: Tuning techniques
bullets: Narrow filters to specific known-good parents, paths or accounts, not broad exclusions
Raise thresholds in correlation rules carefully and record why
Enrich alerts with asset criticality so low-value noise can be prioritised down
Split one noisy rule into a high-fidelity alert and a lower-severity hunting query

sections.heading: Beware over-tuning
paragraphs: Every exclusion is a place an attacker can hide. Prefer exclusions that are hard to imitate, such as a signed binary's full path plus its parent, over ones attackers can easily copy.

articles.title: The incident response lifecycle
articles.summary: From preparation to lessons learned, and how NIST's 2025 guidance places response within the wider risk-management picture.

sections.heading: Classic phases
paragraphs: Earlier NIST guidance described incident handling as preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. Many teams still structure playbooks this way.

sections.heading: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (2025)
paragraphs: Revision 3 frames incident response recommendations as a CSF 2.0 Community Profile, so preparation and improvement are connected to the Govern, Identify and Protect functions as well as Detect, Respond and Recover.

sections.heading: What good looks like
bullets: Clear roles and an incident commander
Pre-approved containment actions
Evidence preserved before systems are rebuilt
Lessons learned that change controls, not just documents

articles.title: Evidence collection and chain of custody
articles.summary: Collecting the most volatile evidence first and keeping it trustworthy.

sections.heading: Order of volatility
paragraphs: RFC 3227 recommends collecting evidence from the most to the least volatile: registers and cache, memory and network state, then temporary files, disk, remote logging and finally archival media. Pulling the power destroys memory evidence.

sections.heading: Chain of custody
bullets: Record who collected each item, when, from where and how
Hash evidence at collection and verify the hash before analysis
Store originals read-only and analyse copies

sections.heading: Balance with containment
paragraphs: Sometimes stopping harm matters more than perfect evidence. Decide in advance which systems justify a memory capture before isolation.

articles.title: Segmentation and Zero Trust in practice
articles.summary: Moving from 'trusted internal network' to per-request access decisions.

sections.heading: Principles
paragraphs: NIST SP 800-207 describes Zero Trust as removing implicit trust based on network location. Access to each resource is granted per session, using policy that considers identity, device state and other signals.

sections.heading: Practical steps
bullets: Segment first: block workstation-to-workstation and workstation-to-server admin traffic
Put admin access behind privileged access workstations and strong MFA
Restrict server egress to what each server needs
Route user web traffic through a gateway that evaluates destination reputation

sections.heading: Maturity
paragraphs: CISA's Zero Trust Maturity Model describes progress across identity, devices, networks, applications and data. It is a journey, not a single purchase.

articles.title: The cloud shared responsibility model
articles.summary: Which security tasks the cloud provider handles and which remain yours.

sections.heading: The split
paragraphs: Cloud providers secure the underlying infrastructure. Customers remain responsible for what they put in the cloud and how they configure it. The exact split depends on the service model: you manage more with virtual machines (IaaS) than with fully managed software (SaaS).

sections.heading: Always yours
bullets: Identities and access permissions
Data classification and protection
Configuration of the services you use (for example public storage settings)
Monitoring and responding to activity in your accounts

articles.title: Cloud logging for detection
articles.summary: The control-plane and identity logs that reveal most cloud attacks.

sections.heading: Key sources
bullets: Control-plane audit logs (for example AWS CloudTrail): who changed what, from where
Identity sign-in logs (for example Microsoft Entra ID): authentication results, MFA, conditional access
Service-specific data access logs for storage and databases
Network flow logs for workloads

sections.heading: What to alert on
bullets: New access keys or role assignments for privileged identities
Disabling of logging or security services
Sign-ins from unusual locations followed by permission changes
Storage made public

practice.label: Identity attacks in the threat profiles

articles.title: Security frameworks at a glance
articles.summary: What NIST CSF 2.0, CIS Controls, ISO/IEC 27001, ATT&CK, D3FEND and the Cyber Kill Chain are each for.

sections.heading: Programme frameworks
bullets: NIST CSF 2.0 organises cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover
CIS Critical Security Controls are a prioritised set of safeguards grouped into Implementation Groups for organisations of different sizes
ISO/IEC 27001 specifies requirements for an information security management system and can be certified

sections.heading: Threat-informed frameworks
bullets: MITRE ATT&CK catalogues adversary tactics and techniques
MITRE D3FEND catalogues defensive countermeasure techniques
The Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain describes intrusion phases from reconnaissance to actions on objectives

sections.heading: How they fit together
paragraphs: Programme frameworks say what a security programme should achieve; threat-informed frameworks help decide which threats to prioritise and how to detect and counter them.

practice.label: ATT&CK mapping in the attack library

articles.title: Prioritising vulnerabilities: CVSS, EPSS, KEV and SSVC
articles.summary: Four different signals and the question each one answers.

sections.heading: Different questions
bullets: CVSS (FIRST) rates technical severity: how bad would exploitation be?
EPSS (FIRST) estimates the probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days
CISA KEV lists vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild
SSVC (CISA) is a decision tree that adds your own context, such as exposure and mission impact

sections.heading: Combine them
paragraphs: Severity alone produces too many 'critical' items. Exploitation evidence (KEV) and likelihood (EPSS), weighed against asset exposure and business impact, focus effort where attacks are actually happening.

practice.label: CVE snapshot with all three signals

articles.title: Building a career in security operations
articles.summary: Roles, skills and how to show practical ability.

sections.heading: Roles
paragraphs: NIST's NICE Workforce Framework describes cybersecurity work roles and the knowledge and skills they need. Common SOC-related roles include defensive cybersecurity analysis, incident response and threat analysis.

sections.heading: Skills that transfer
bullets: Operating systems and networking fundamentals
Reading logs and writing queries
Scripting for automation (for example Python or PowerShell)
Clear written communication of findings

sections.heading: Show, don't just tell
paragraphs: Projects with honest documentation (what you built, what you tested, what you did not do) demonstrate ability. Certifications are offered by several bodies; check which ones employers in your target region actually ask for rather than collecting them.

articles.title: Building a safe home lab
articles.summary: Practising detection and response without risk to anyone else.

sections.heading: Isolation and permission
paragraphs: Keep attack simulations inside networks and systems you own, isolated from your home and work networks. Never test against systems you do not have written permission to test.

sections.heading: A starter lab
bullets: A hypervisor with a Windows client, a Windows server (domain controller) and a Linux host
Sysmon on Windows hosts and log forwarding to an open-source SIEM
A small network sensor (Zeek or Suricata) on the lab network
Snapshots so you can reset after each exercise

sections.heading: Exercises
bullets: Generate failed logons and build a brute-force alert
Run a benign PowerShell download in the lab and find it in script block logs
Write a Sigma rule and test it against your own events
